hook: The two tidal bulges you were taught in school do not exist.
the_question: If the Moon pulls the ocean toward it, why is there also a high tide on the far side of the Earth?
the_intuition: The textbook answer is two static bulges: one under the Moon, one opposite it, with the Earth rotating beneath them.
mechanism: For a bulge to stay under the Moon it would have to travel around the Earth at roughly 1,600 km/h.
Shallow-water waves in a 4 km ocean cap out near 700 km/h. The water can never keep up with the Moon.
why_it_matters: Tides are a shallow-water wave problem, not a static-shape problem — the ocean sloshes in basins rather than bulging.
the_catch: Newton's forcing function is right; only his response model is wrong. This is not 'Newton was wrong about gravity'.
caption: The two tidal bulges in every textbook diagram are not what the ocean actually does. Which piece of school science surprised you most when it turned out to be wrong?
alt_text: An eight-slide carousel explaining why the two static tidal bulges taught in school do not exist, and why tides are a shallow-water wave problem instead.

es.hook: Los dos abultamientos de marea que te enseñaron en la escuela no existen.
es.the_question: Si la Luna atrae el océano hacia ella, ¿por qué hay también marea alta en el lado opuesto de la Tierra?
es.the_intuition: La respuesta de los libros son dos abultamientos estáticos: uno bajo la Luna, otro enfrente, con la Tierra girando debajo.
mechanism: Para quedarse bajo la Luna, un abultamiento tendría que recorrer la Tierra a unos 1.600 km/h.
Las ondas en aguas someras de un océano de 4 km se topan cerca de 700 km/h. El agua nunca alcanza a la Luna.
es.why_it_matters: Las mareas son un problema de ondas en aguas someras, no de forma estática: el océano oscila en cuencas en vez de abultarse.
es.the_catch: La función forzante de Newton es correcta; solo su modelo de respuesta es erróneo. Esto no es "Newton se equivocó sobre la gravedad".
